title: Apple's Claris Testing 'Harbor' App for Local AI on Macs
content:
Apple's Claris subsidiary is testing an app called Harbor, which turns Apple silicon Macs into a private AI server.
Harbor works with a single Apple silicon Mac, but it also supports connecting multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory for larger models. Apple added RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 with macOS Tahoe 26.2, making clustering faster.
Harbor detects devices connected over Thunderbolt 5 and lets users browse for, download, and load open-weight models. It's described as an easy-to-use app with no manual configuration required.
Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency than a single computer can handle alone.
Set up in minutes, not hours. Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you're running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.
Download and run models directly. Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.
Cluster for scale. Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer's capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.
Harbor is in early access and is not publicly available. There was an App Store listing, but it has now been removed.
Claris is known for its database platform FileMaker, which is aimed at businesses, so it isn't clear how Apple will market the Harbor app or whether it will be free. The sign-up page for Harbor asks for a company name, which suggests more of a business focus.
There are already well-known, free alternatives for Mac users who want to run a local AI server. Exo is an open-source tool for clustering Macs, and LM Studio is available for single-Mac use, but Apple's Harbor app appears to combine LM Studio's simple interface with clustering.

report.summary: Apple's Claris subsidiary is testing Harbor, an early-access app that turns Apple silicon Macs into private local AI inference servers and clusters them over Thunderbolt 5.
report.background: Apple silicon's unified memory architecture has quietly made Macs one of the best consumer platforms for running open-weight language models locally: a high-end Mac can hold tens of gigabytes of model weights in the same memory pool the GPU uses. That has spawned a fast-growing hobbyist and prosumer ecosystem around tools like LM Studio, Ollama and the open-source clustering project Exo. Meanwhile, Apple added RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 in macOS Tahoe 26.2, which makes linking Macs into a low-latency cluster practical rather than experimental. Harbor appears to be Apple's attempt to package these capabilities into a polished product. Notably, it is being built at Claris, the wholly owned subsidiary best known for FileMaker, suggesting a commercial or business-oriented rather than consumer framing. The timing also reflects competitive pressure from high-memory PCs and dedicated AI appliances aimed at teams that want capable local inference without cloud costs or data leaving the building.
key_points: Harbor is a one-stop app that makes a single Apple silicon Mac act as a private AI server. You browse, download and load open-weight models from inside the app, and inference runs entirely on your hardware with nothing sent to the cloud. The pitch is setup in minutes with no command line and no infrastructure expertise.

The headline feature is clustering. Harbor automatically detects other Thunderbolt 5 Macs and pools their unified memory into one inference resource, letting you run models too large for any single machine or serve more concurrent requests. Apple's new RDMA support over Thunderbolt 5 in macOS Tahoe 26.2 makes that link fast enough to be useful.

Harbor is in early access and is not publicly available; an App Store listing briefly appeared and was then pulled. That pattern suggests a controlled pilot rather than a launch, and details on pricing, release timing and supported Macs remain unconfirmed.

The business angle is unusually explicit. Claris is the FileMaker database company, and Harbor's sign-up page asks for a company name, implying an enterprise or team product rather than a free consumer utility. How Apple markets it, and whether it ships free with macOS, is still unknown.

Free alternatives already exist. Exo open-sources Mac clustering, while LM Studio offers a polished single-Mac interface. Harbor's apparent differentiator is combining LM Studio-style simplicity with automatic multi-machine clustering in one first-party app.
report.impact: For the AI industry, a first-party Apple clustering tool is a signal that local inference is moving from hobbyist tinkering toward supported infrastructure, potentially giving privacy-sensitive enterprises a credible alternative to cloud APIs. For developers, Harbor could lower the barrier to running large open-weight models on hardware teams already own, though a closed, business-focused app may frustrate those who prefer the flexibility of Exo, llama.cpp or MLX. For regular users, the near-term effect is limited, since this is early access and Mac-only. The bigger question is whether Apple bundles local model serving into macOS, which would normalize on-device AI and put pressure on cloud-centric competitors.
report.tools: To explore the same ideas today: LM Studio for a polished single-Mac chat and server interface; Ollama for a scriptable local model runner; Exo for open-source Thunderbolt-based Mac clustering; and Apple's MLX framework plus mlx-lm for developers who want to build directly on Apple silicon. llama.cpp remains the most portable inference engine. If you plan to cluster, note that Thunderbolt 5 hardware and macOS Tahoe 26.2 or later are central to Harbor's approach.
